claim: SUMOs are conjugated to proteins to regulate a variety of cellular processes.
source: Small ubiquitin-related modifiers (SUMOs) are conjugated to proteins to regulate a variety of cellular processes.
evidence: This is a general statement about SUMO function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: SENPs are cysteine proteases with a catalytic center located within a channel between two subdomains.
source: SENPs are cysteine proteases with a catalytic center located within a channel between two subdomains that catalyzes SUMO C-terminal cleavage for processing of SUMO precursors and de-SUMOylation of target proteins.
evidence: This is a structural and functional characterization of SENPs based on established knowledge.

claim: SENPs catalyze SUMO C-terminal cleavage for processing of SUMO precursors and de-SUMOylation of target proteins.
source: SENPs are cysteine proteases with a catalytic center located within a channel between two subdomains that catalyzes SUMO C-terminal cleavage for processing of SUMO precursors and de-SUMOylation of target proteins.
evidence: This describes the enzymatic function of SENPs based on established knowledge.

claim: The β-grasp domain of SUMOs binds to an exosite cleft on SENPs.
source: The β-grasp domain of SUMOs binds to an exosite cleft, and allosterically activates SENPs via an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by prior knowledge and the study's investigation.

claim: The β-grasp domain allosterically activates SENPs.
source: The β-grasp domain of SUMOs binds to an exosite cleft, and allosterically activates SENPs via an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is an established observation in the field that the study aims to explain mechanistically.

claim: Binding of the β-grasp domain induces significant conformational and dynamic changes in SENP1.
source: Our molecular dynamics simulations showed that binding of the β-grasp domain induces significant conformational and dynamic changes in SENP1, including widening of the exosite cleft and quenching of nanosecond dynamics in all but a distal region.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MD simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Binding of the β-grasp domain causes widening of the exosite cleft in SENP1.
source: Our molecular dynamics simulations showed that binding of the β-grasp domain induces significant conformational and dynamic changes in SENP1, including widening of the exosite cleft and quenching of nanosecond dynamics in all but a distal region.
evidence: This is directly observed in the MD simulations as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Binding of the β-grasp domain causes quenching of nanosecond dynamics in all but a distal region of SENP1.
source: Our molecular dynamics simulations showed that binding of the β-grasp domain induces significant conformational and dynamic changes in SENP1, including widening of the exosite cleft and quenching of nanosecond dynamics in all but a distal region.
evidence: This is directly observed in the MD simulations as shown in Figure 3.

claim: SUMOylation is involved in various cellular processes and required for normal growth and development in all eukaryotes.
source: Whereas conjugation with ubiquitin targets proteins for degradation, conjugation with small ubiquitin-related modifiers (SUMOs), or SUMOylation, is involved in various cellular processes and required for normal growth and development in all eukaryotes (Johnson, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Johnson, 2004.

claim: There is only 18% sequence identity between ubiquitin and SUMO1.
source: Although there is only 18% sequence identity between ubiquitin and SUMO1 (the founding member of the SUMO family [Okura et al., 1996]), their structured domains share a common fold known as β-grasp, in which five β-strands wrap around an α-helix (Bayer et al., 1998) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about sequence identity supported by citation to Okura et al., 1996.

claim: SUMO1 is the founding member of the SUMO family.
source: Although there is only 18% sequence identity between ubiquitin and SUMO1 (the founding member of the SUMO family [Okura et al., 1996]), their structured domains share a common fold known as β-grasp, in which five β-strands wrap around an α-helix (Bayer et al., 1998) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Okura et al., 1996.

claim: The structured domains of ubiquitin and SUMO1 share a common fold known as β-grasp.
source: Although there is only 18% sequence identity between ubiquitin and SUMO1 (the founding member of the SUMO family [Okura et al., 1996]), their structured domains share a common fold known as β-grasp, in which five β-strands wrap around an α-helix (Bayer et al., 1998) (Figure 1).
evidence: This structural observation is supported by citation to Bayer et al., 1998.

claim: The β-grasp fold consists of five β-strands wrapping around an α-helix.
source: Although there is only 18% sequence identity between ubiquitin and SUMO1 (the founding member of the SUMO family [Okura et al., 1996]), their structured domains share a common fold known as β-grasp, in which five β-strands wrap around an α-helix (Bayer et al., 1998) (Figure 1).
evidence: This structural description is supported by citation to Bayer et al., 1998 and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: SUMOylation occurs through an isopeptide linkage between a conserved Gly-Gly motif at the C-terminus of SUMOs and a lysine sidechain on target proteins.
source: SUMOylation, like ubiquitination, is through an isopeptide linkage between a conserved Gly-Gly motif at the C-terminus of SUMOs and a lysine sidechain on target proteins.
evidence: This describes the biochemical mechanism of SUMOylation based on established knowledge.

claim: All SUMOs are translated as precursors that are first processed by SENPs.
source: All SUMOs are translated as precursors that are first processed by the SENP family of SUMO-specific proteases, whereby a short C-terminal extension is cleaved to expose the reactive Gly-Gly motif.
evidence: This describes the SUMO maturation process based on established knowledge.

claim: SENP processing of SUMO precursors involves cleavage of a short C-terminal extension to expose the reactive Gly-Gly motif.
source: All SUMOs are translated as precursors that are first processed by the SENP family of SUMO-specific proteases, whereby a short C-terminal extension is cleaved to expose the reactive Gly-Gly motif.
evidence: This describes the specific enzymatic action of SENPs based on established knowledge.

claim: SUMOylation is reversible.
source: Like the much better-known posttranslational modification phosphorylation, SUMOylation is reversible, and de-SUMOylation is also catalyzed by SENPs (Yeh, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeh, 2009.

claim: De-SUMOylation is catalyzed by SENPs.
source: Like the much better-known posttranslational modification phosphorylation, SUMOylation is reversible, and de-SUMOylation is also catalyzed by SENPs (Yeh, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeh, 2009.

claim: The catalytic activity of SENPs on short peptide substrates is low.
source: The catalytic activity of SENPs on short peptide substrates is low, likely to avoid off-target cleavage, and is substantially enhanced by the β-grasp domain of SUMOs (Mikolajczyk et al., 2007).
evidence: This observation is supported by citation to Mikolajczyk et al., 2007.

claim: The low catalytic activity of SENPs on short peptide substrates is likely to avoid off-target cleavage.
source: The catalytic activity of SENPs on short peptide substrates is low, likely to avoid off-target cleavage, and is substantially enhanced by the β-grasp domain of SUMOs (Mikolajczyk et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed low activity.

claim: The catalytic activity of SENPs on short peptide substrates is substantially enhanced by the β-grasp domain of SUMOs.
source: The catalytic activity of SENPs on short peptide substrates is low, likely to avoid off-target cleavage, and is substantially enhanced by the β-grasp domain of SUMOs (Mikolajczyk et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mikolajczyk et al., 2007.

claim: The human genome encodes three SUMOs (SUMO1, SUMO2, and SUMO3).
source: The human genome encodes three SUMOs (SUMO1, SUMO2, and SUMO3) and six SUMO-specific SENPs (SENP1, SENP2, SENP3, SENP5, SENP6, and SENP7).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the human genome.

claim: The human genome encodes six SUMO-specific SENPs (SENP1, SENP2, SENP3, SENP5, SENP6, and SENP7).
source: The human genome encodes three SUMOs (SUMO1, SUMO2, and SUMO3) and six SUMO-specific SENPs (SENP1, SENP2, SENP3, SENP5, SENP6, and SENP7).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the human genome.

claim: SENPs belong to the cysteine protease superfamily.
source: SENPs belong to the cysteine protease superfamily, and regulate both physiological and pathological processes mediated by SUMOylated proteins (Yeh, 2009).
evidence: This is a classification supported by citation to Yeh, 2009.

claim: SENPs regulate both physiological and pathological processes mediated by SUMOylated proteins.
source: SENPs belong to the cysteine protease superfamily, and regulate both physiological and pathological processes mediated by SUMOylated proteins (Yeh, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeh, 2009.

claim: Hypoxia induces the nuclear entry and SUMOylation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α).
source: As an example, hypoxia (i.e., low oxygen), a condition common to fetal development and tumorigenesis, induces the nuclear entry and SUMOylation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) (Cheng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2007.

claim: SUMOylated HIF1α is subject to ubiquitin-dependent degradation.
source: SUMOylated HIF1α is subject to ubiquitin-dependent degradation, and hence deSUMOylation of HIF1α by SENP1 is central to hypoxia response.
evidence: This describes a regulatory mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: DeSUMOylation of HIF1α by SENP1 is central to hypoxia response.
source: SUMOylated HIF1α is subject to ubiquitin-dependent degradation, and hence deSUMOylation of HIF1α by SENP1 is central to hypoxia response.
evidence: This is an inference from the degradation mechanism and SENP1's role.

claim: SENP1 is overexpressed during the development of prostate cancer.
source: For this and other reasons SENP1 is overexpressed during the development of prostate cancer, and has emerged as a potential therapeutic target (Cheng et al., 2006; Bawa-Khalfe et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2006; Bawa-Khalfe et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013.

claim: SENP1 has emerged as a potential therapeutic target.
source: For this and other reasons SENP1 is overexpressed during the development of prostate cancer, and has emerged as a potential therapeutic target (Cheng et al., 2006; Bawa-Khalfe et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2006; Bawa-Khalfe et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Several types of SENP inhibitors have been identified, including SUMO variants or C-terminal fragments tethered with electrophilic traps.
source: Several types of SENP inhibitors have been identified, including SUMO variants or C-terminal fragments tethered with electrophilic traps (Hemelaar et al., 2004; Borodovsky et al., 2005; Dobrota et al., 2012) and small molecules (Albrow et al., 2011; Ponder et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012; Madu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hemelaar et al., 2004; Borodovsky et al., 2005; Dobrota et al., 2012.

claim: Small molecule SENP inhibitors have been identified.
source: Several types of SENP inhibitors have been identified, including SUMO variants or C-terminal fragments tethered with electrophilic traps (Hemelaar et al., 2004; Borodovsky et al., 2005; Dobrota et al., 2012) and small molecules (Albrow et al., 2011; Ponder et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012; Madu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albrow et al., 2011; Ponder et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012; Madu et al., 2013.

claim: The therapeutic value of SENP inhibitors is limited by covalent linkage with the catalytic cysteine residue, low specificity, or low potency.
source: The therapeutic value of these inhibitors is limited by covalent linkage with the catalytic cysteine residue, low specificity, or low potency.
evidence: This is an assessment of current inhibitors based on their known properties.

claim: SENP catalytic domains only undergo localized conformational rearrangements upon binding SUMOs.
source: Structural studies have shown that SENP catalytic domains only undergo localized conformational rearrangements upon binding SUMOs (as precursors, processed products, or SUMO conjugates), and that SENP-SUMO interactions are largely similar during precursor processing and deSUMOylation (Reverter and Lima, 2004, 2006; Shen et al., 2006a, 2006b; Xu et al., 2006; Alegre and Reverter, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: SENP-SUMO interactions are largely similar during precursor processing and deSUMOylation.
source: Structural studies have shown that SENP catalytic domains only undergo localized conformational rearrangements upon binding SUMOs (as precursors, processed products, or SUMO conjugates), and that SENP-SUMO interactions are largely similar during precursor processing and deSUMOylation (Reverter and Lima, 2004, 2006; Shen et al., 2006a, 2006b; Xu et al., 2006; Alegre and Reverter, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: The catalytic triad in SENP1 comprises residues His533, Asp550, and Cys603.
source: In SENP1, the catalytic triad comprises residues His533, Asp550, and Cys603 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a structural fact illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The SENP1 catalytic domain consists of residues 419–644.
source: The catalytic domain (residues 419–644) consists of eight α-helices and seven β-strands, divided into two subdomains.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established knowledge.

claim: The SENP1 catalytic domain consists of eight α-helices and seven β-strands, divided into two subdomains.
source: The catalytic domain (residues 419–644) consists of eight α-helices and seven β-strands, divided into two subdomains.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established knowledge.

claim: The lower subdomain of SENP1 contains the α1, α2, and α8 helices and the β1-β2 hairpin.
source: The lower subdomain contains the α1, α2, and α8 helices and the β1-β2 hairpin, while the upper subdomain contains the α4-α6 helices and the β3-β7 sheet.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established knowledge.

claim: The upper subdomain of SENP1 contains the α4-α6 helices and the β3-β7 sheet.
source: The lower subdomain contains the α1, α2, and α8 helices and the β1-β2 hairpin, while the upper subdomain contains the α4-α6 helices and the β3-β7 sheet.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established knowledge.

claim: The α3 and α7 helices glue the two subdomains of SENP1 and form the bottom of the catalytic channel.
source: The two remaining helices, α3 and α7, glue the two subdomains and also form the bottom of a channel where the extended C-terminus of SUMO1 lies and the catalytic triad is situated.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established knowledge.

claim: Three loops line the catalytic channel in SENP1 and likely undergo transient motions during the entrance of the SUMO C-terminus into the channel.
source: Three loops, including residues 464–466 between α2 and α3, residues 530–533 between β4 and β5, and residues 599–602 between β7 and α7, line the channel and likely undergo transient motions during the entrance of the SUMO C-terminus into the channel.
evidence: This is a structural observation combined with speculation about dynamics.

claim: Trp534 floors the substrate in the SENP1 catalytic channel.
source: One tryptophan residue, Trp534, floors the substrate while another, Trp465, forms a lid over its conserved Gly-Gly motif.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established knowledge.

claim: Trp465 forms a lid over the conserved Gly-Gly motif of the substrate in SENP1.
source: One tryptophan residue, Trp534, floors the substrate while another, Trp465, forms a lid over its conserved Gly-Gly motif.
evidence: This is a structural description based on established knowledge.

claim: The burial of the catalytic center in the channel and the transient motions around the channel necessary for proper alignment of the substrate may contribute to the low catalytic activity of SENPs on short peptides.
source: The burial of the catalytic center in the channel and consequently the transient motions around the channel necessary for proper alignment of the substrate with respect to the catalytic center may contribute to the low catalytic activity of SENPs on short peptides.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed low activity.

claim: The β-grasp domain of SUMO1 binds into a large cleft (the exosite) on SENP1.
source: The β-grasp domain of SUMO1 binds into a large cleft to the side (hereafter the exosite), and makes separate contacts with the two subdomains of SENP1: the β1-β2 hairpin in the lower subdomain and the α4-α5 helices in the upper subdomain (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The β-grasp domain of SUMO1 makes separate contacts with the β1-β2 hairpin in the lower subdomain and the α4-α5 helices in the upper subdomain of SENP1.
source: The β-grasp domain of SUMO1 binds into a large cleft to the side (hereafter the exosite), and makes separate contacts with the two subdomains of SENP1: the β1-β2 hairpin in the lower subdomain and the α4-α5 helices in the upper subdomain (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: An insertion in the β1-β2 hairpin of SENP2 that extended the interface with SUMO2 resulted in no other change in the structure of the catalytic domain but nevertheless increased its catalytic activity.
source: An insertion in the β1-β2 hairpin of SENP2 that extended the interface with SUMO2 resulted in no other change in the structure of the catalytic domain but nevertheless increased its catalytic activity (Alegre and Reverter, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alegre and Reverter, 2014.

claim: Changes in conformational dynamics can mediate allosteric effects.
source: In this context, we note that, in addition to conformational changes, the possibility that changes in conformational dynamics can mediate allosteric effects has received attention in the recent literature (Guo and Zhou, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo and Zhou, 2016.

claim: Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) in the cysteine protease class have very low catalytic activity on short peptide substrates.
source: Similar to SENPs, deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) in the cysteine protease class also have very low catalytic activity on short peptide substrates (Dang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dang et al., 1998.

claim: The catalytic domains of DUBs in different families all contain a catalytic channel that bears resemblance to that in SENPs.
source: Although the catalytic domains of DUBs in different families have different structural scaffolds, they all contain a catalytic channel that bears resemblance to that in SENPs (Hu et al., 2002; Misaghi et al., 2005; Messick et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2002; Misaghi et al., 2005; Messick et al., 2008.

claim: The positioning of the ubiquitin domain in the exosite of DUBs resembles that of the SUMO β-grasp domain in SENPs.
source: The resemblance further extends to the positioning of the ubiquitin domain in the exosite.
evidence: This is an inference from structural similarities.

claim: Allosteric activation mechanisms of SENPs and DUBs may share certain similarities.
source: It may thus be expected that allosteric activation mechanisms of SENPs and DUBs share certain similarities.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural similarities.

claim: A pre-bound β-grasp domain (as contained in truncated SUMO1) can enhance the SENP1 catalytic activity on a short peptide substrate.
source: A major step toward elucidating the allosteric activation of SENP1 by the β-grasp domain of SUMO1 was taken in a recent study (Chen et al., 2014). These authors confirmed the ability of a pre-bound β-grasp domain, as contained in a truncated SUMO1 construct (residues 1–92, hereafter referred to as trunSUMO1), to enhance the SENP1 catalytic activity on a short peptide substrate, and further traced the enhancement solely to an increase in kcat.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: The enhancement of SENP1 catalytic activity by the β-grasp domain is solely due to an increase in kcat.
source: A major step toward elucidating the allosteric activation of SENP1 by the β-grasp domain of SUMO1 was taken in a recent study (Chen et al., 2014). These authors confirmed the ability of a pre-bound β-grasp domain, as contained in a truncated SUMO1 construct (residues 1–92, hereafter referred to as trunSUMO1), to enhance the SENP1 catalytic activity on a short peptide substrate, and further traced the enhancement solely to an increase in kcat.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: TrunSUMO1 binding yields a gradient in backbone amide chemical shift perturbations emanating from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center.
source: Their NMR data showed that trunSUMO1 binding yielded a gradient in backbone amide chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) emanating from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data from Chen et al., 2014.

claim: Significant sidechain methyl CSPs were observed on six residues (Leu450, Val501, Val509, V516, Val518, and ValV532) upon trunSUMO1 binding.
source: Significant sidechain methyl CSPs were also observed on six residues that dotted the region from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center, which indicated to the authors that the allosteric effect was propagated through the hydrophobic core.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data from Chen et al., 2014.

claim: The allosteric effect in SENP1 is propagated through the hydrophobic core.
source: Significant sidechain methyl CSPs were also observed on six residues that dotted the region from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center, which indicated to the authors that the allosteric effect was propagated through the hydrophobic core.
evidence: This is an interpretation by Chen et al., 2014 based on their NMR data.

claim: TrunSUMO1 binding enhanced microsecond-millisecond dynamics for residues around the catalytic center.
source: Their Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) relaxation dispersion data showed that trunSUMO1 binding enhanced microsecond-millisecond (μs-ms) dynamics for residues around the catalytic center, suggesting a realignment of these residues.
evidence: This is supported by CPMG data from Chen et al., 2014.

claim: Enhanced μs-ms dynamics around the catalytic center suggests a realignment of these residues.
source: Their Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) relaxation dispersion data showed that trunSUMO1 binding enhanced microsecond-millisecond (μs-ms) dynamics for residues around the catalytic center, suggesting a realignment of these residues.
evidence: This is an interpretation by Chen et al., 2014 based on their CPMG data.

claim: Three replicate explicit-solvent MD simulations were carried out for apo SENP1, SENP1 bound with trunSUMO1, and SENP1 bound with full-length SUMO1 precursor.
source: We carried out three replicate explicit-solvent MD simulations for apo SENP1, for SENP1 bound with trunSUMO1, and for SENP1 bound with the full-length SUMO1 precursor (referred to as preSUMO1 hereafter).
evidence: This describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: Each system accumulated 1.7 μs of total simulation time across three replicate simulations.
source: For each system, the three simulations accumulated 1.7 μs of total time and are denoted as sim1, sim2, and sim3.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: The apo form of SENP1 samples disconnected free energy basins, in contrast to the two bound forms.
source: The apo form samples disconnected free energy basins, in contrast to the two bound forms, indicating a decrease in flexibility upon β-grasp binding (see below).
evidence: This is observed from principal component analysis of the MD simulations.

claim: There is a decrease in flexibility of SENP1 upon β-grasp binding.
source: The apo form samples disconnected free energy basins, in contrast to the two bound forms, indicating a decrease in flexibility upon β-grasp binding (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the principal component analysis of the MD simulations.

claim: Both PC1 and PC2 feature prominent displacements in the two exosite interface regions and in the loops lining the catalytic channel.
source: Both PC1 and PC2 feature prominent displacements in the two exosite interface regions and in the loops lining the catalytic channel (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is observed from principal component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Relative to the apo form, the two bound forms move along positive PC1 and PC2.
source: Relative to the apo form, the two bound forms move along positive PC1 and PC2, both of which involve the moving apart between the two interface regions and the opposite movements of loopA and loopB with respect to the β-grasp domain.
evidence: This is observed from principal component analysis of the MD simulations.

claim: The mean cleft distance changes from 22.4 ± 1.5 Å for the apo form to 23.1 ± 0.5 Å for the trunSUMO1-bound form.
source: The mean and standard deviation of the cleft distance change from 22.4 ± 1.5 Å for the apo form to 23.1 ± 0.5 Å and 22.6 ± 1.5 Å for the trunSUMO1-bound and preSUMO1-bound forms, respectively, indicating widening of the exosite cleft upon β-grasp binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is measured from the MD simulations as shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The mean cleft distance changes from 22.4 ± 1.5 Å for the apo form to 22.6 ± 1.5 Å for the preSUMO1-bound form.
source: The mean and standard deviation of the cleft distance change from 22.4 ± 1.5 Å for the apo form to 23.1 ± 0.5 Å and 22.6 ± 1.5 Å for the trunSUMO1-bound and preSUMO1-bound forms, respectively, indicating widening of the exosite cleft upon β-grasp binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is measured from the MD simulations as shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Relative to the apo form, the two bound forms show loopA moving away from the exosite cleft and toward the upper subdomain.
source: Relative to the apo form, the two bound form show similar movements for both loopA and loopB, the former away from the exosite cleft (i.e., decreasing x) and toward the upper subdomain (i.e., increasing y) while the latter toward the cleft and away from the channel (i.e., increasing x and y); loopC moves in opposite directions in the two bound forms but perhaps that is accidental due to the long distance from the binding interface.
evidence: This is observed from the MD simulations as shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Relative to the apo form, the two bound forms show loopB moving toward the cleft and away from the channel.
source: Relative to the apo form, the two bound form show similar movements for both loopA and loopB, the former away from the exosite cleft (i.e., decreasing x) and toward the upper subdomain (i.e., increasing y) while the latter toward the cleft and away from the channel (i.e., increasing x and y); loopC moves in opposite directions in the two bound forms but perhaps that is accidental due to the long distance from the binding interface.
evidence: This is observed from the MD simulations as shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The movement of loopA toward α7 leads to stronger inter-subdomain contact.
source: The movement of loopA (toward α7) leads to stronger inter-subdomain contact; the x component of loopB's movement has a similar effect, while the y component may create space for the docking of the proximal portion of a C-terminus when tethered to the β-grasp domain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed movements from the MD simulations.

claim: The y component of loopB's movement may create space for the docking of the proximal portion of a C-terminus when tethered to the β-grasp domain.
source: The movement of loopA (toward α7) leads to stronger inter-subdomain contact; the x component of loopB's movement has a similar effect, while the y component may create space for the docking of the proximal portion of a C-terminus when tethered to the β-grasp domain.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed movements from the MD simulations.

claim: In apo SENP1, the W465 sidechain samples a broad range of positions.
source: In apo SENP1 this sidechain samples a broad range of positions, but in preSUMO1-bound SENP1 it stays stably near the top of α7 (on the sub-μs timescale); the situation is intermediate in trunSUMO1-bound SENP1.
evidence: This is observed from the MD simulations as shown in Figure 2d.

claim: In preSUMO1-bound SENP1, the W465 sidechain stays stably near the top of α7 on the sub-μs timescale.
source: In apo SENP1 this sidechain samples a broad range of positions, but in preSUMO1-bound SENP1 it stays stably near the top of α7 (on the sub-μs timescale); the situation is intermediate in trunSUMO1-bound SENP1.
evidence: This is observed from the MD simulations as shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Relative to apo SENP1, the two bound forms both show decreased flexibility throughout most of the amino acid sequence, except for the N- and C-terminal segments.
source: Relative to apo SENP1, the two bound forms both show decreased flexibility throughout most of the amino acid sequence, except for the N- and C-terminal segments (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is observed from RMSF analysis of the MD simulations shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In both trunSUMO1-bound and preSUMO1-bound forms, rigidification propagates from the exosite cleft to the entire upper subdomain and to most of the lower subdomain.
source: In both systems, rigidification propagates from the exosite cleft to the entire upper subdomain and to most of the lower subdomain.
evidence: This is observed from RMSF analysis of the MD simulations shown in Figure 3b,c.

claim: The rigidification upon β-grasp binding is compensated to some extent by higher flexibility in the distal region of the lower subdomain, comprising the N- and C-terminal segments.
source: The rigidification is compensated to some extent by higher flexibility in the distal region of the lower subdomain, comprising the N- and C-terminal segments.
evidence: This is observed from RMSF analysis of the MD simulations shown in Figure 3b,c.

claim: Calculated backbone amide CSPs agree well with the experimental data of Chen et al. (2014) but are more pronounced.
source: Overall, they agree well with the experimental data, but are more pronounced.
evidence: This is a comparison between calculated CSPs from MD simulations and experimental NMR data.

claim: The calculated backbone amide CSPs spread all the way to the back in both subdomains.
source: The calculated backbone amide CSPs spread all the way to the back, in both subdomains.
evidence: This is observed from CSP calculations on the MD simulations shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The calculation identifies three of the six experimentally detected residues as having significant sidechain methyl CSPs.
source: The calculation identifies three of the six experimentally detected residues as well as 12 others as having significant sidechain methyl CSPs (>0.08 ppm).
evidence: This is observed from CSP calculations on the MD simulations shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The calculation identifies 12 additional residues (beyond the six experimentally detected) as having significant sidechain methyl CSPs.
source: The calculation identifies three of the six experimentally detected residues as well as 12 others as having significant sidechain methyl CSPs (>0.08 ppm).
evidence: This is observed from CSP calculations on the MD simulations shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Two hydrophobic pathways emerge from the calculated sidechain methyl CSPs, each connecting an exosite interface region in one subdomain to the catalytic center.
source: Interestingly, with the 12 additional residues, two hydrophobic pathways emerge, each connecting an exosite interface region in one subdomain to the catalytic center.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of calculated CSPs shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Chemical shifts are a measure of both conformational and dynamics effects.
source: Chemical shifts are a measure of both conformational and dynamics effects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMR chemical shifts.

claim: The sidechain methyl CSPs are a manifestation of the conformational and dynamic changes induced by β-grasp binding.
source: Hence the sidechain methyl CSPs are a manifestation of the conformational and dynamic changes induced by β-grasp binding, and the hydrophobic pathways may represent short paths over which allosteric effects are propagated from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the calculated CSPs.

claim: The hydrophobic pathways may represent short paths over which allosteric effects are propagated from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center.
source: Hence the sidechain methyl CSPs are a manifestation of the conformational and dynamic changes induced by β-grasp binding, and the hydrophobic pathways may represent short paths over which allosteric effects are propagated from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the calculated CSPs.

claim: Very similar community structures are obtained from the replicate simulations of each system.
source: Very similar community structures are obtained from the replicate simulations of each system, so here we focus on sim1.
evidence: This is observed from community analysis of the MD simulations.

claim: Five major communities can be recognized for SENP1 in all cases.
source: In all cases, five major communities (numbered 1 to 5) can be recognized for SENP1, anchored by β1β2 and α2; α3; α4α5; α6 and various parts of β4–β7; and α7, respectively, and possibly containing other segments.
evidence: This is observed from community analysis of the MD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the apo form, four minor communities (numbered 1′, 2′, 4′, and 4″) are formed in addition to the five major communities.
source: In the apo form, in addition to these five major communities, four minor communities (numbered 1′, 2′, 4′, and 4″) are also formed.
evidence: This is observed from community analysis of the MD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the trunSUMO1-SENP1 complex, SENP1 is partitioned only to the five major communities, with the minor communities absorbed.
source: In the trunSUMO1-SENP1 complex, SENP1 is partitioned only to the five major communities, with the minor communities absorbed.
evidence: This is observed from community analysis of the MD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Communities 4, 4′, and 4″ in apo SENP1 coalesce into a single community upon trunSUMO1 binding.
source: In particular, communities 4, 4′, and 4″ in apo SENP1 coalesce into a single community upon trunSUMO1 binding.
evidence: This is observed from community analysis of the MD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The inter-community betweennesses are strengthened upon trunSUMO1 binding, especially between communities 2 and 5 and communities 1 and 4.
source: Moreover, the inter-community betweennesses are also strengthened, especially between the two communities, 2 and 5, anchored by the two central helices (α3 and α7, respectively) and community 1 in the lower subdomain and community 4 in the upper subdomain.
evidence: This is observed from community analysis of the MD simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The strengthened inter-community coupling is in line with the stronger inter-subdomain contact.
source: This strengthened inter-community coupling is in line with the stronger inter-subdomain contact noted above.
evidence: This is an inference connecting two observations from the MD simulations.

claim: The β-grasp domain couples strongly to both subdomains.
source: It comes about because the β-grasp domain couples strongly to both subdomains.
evidence: This is inferred from the community analysis of the MD simulations.

claim: The β-grasp domain, by serving as a bridge linking the two exosite interface regions, strengthens the motional coupling both within and between the subdomains of SENP1.
source: Therefore, the β-grasp domain, by serving as a bridge linking the two exosite interface regions, strengthens the motional coupling both within and between the subdomains of SENP1.
evidence: This is inferred from the community analysis of the MD simulations.

claim: A similar bridging role was identified for a peptide in inducing inter-domain allosteric communication in Pin1.
source: A similar bridging role was identified for a peptide in inducing inter-domain allosteric communication in Pin1 (Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2015.

claim: The path lengths from the two exosite interface regions to the catalytic center are shorter in the trunSUMO1-bound form than in the apo form.
source: Indeed, the path lengths from the two exosite interface regions to the catalytic center are shorter in the trunSUMO1-bound form than in the apo form.
evidence: This is observed from path length analysis of the MD simulations.

claim: The simultaneous occurrence of strengthened intra- and inter-subdomain coupling and quenching of ns dynamics observed on SENP1 upon binding an allosteric activator conforms to a pattern previously recognized from other proteins.
source: The simultaneous occurrence of strengthened intra- and inter-subdomain coupling and quenching of ns dynamics observed here on SENP1 upon binding an allosteric activator conforms to a pattern previously recognized from a number of other proteins (including Pin1) in which conformational dynamics plays a prominent role in mediating allosteric communication (Guo and Zhou, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo and Zhou, 2015.

claim: According to a dynamic model of allostery, fast motions are uncorrelated and an allosteric activator strengthens inter-community coupling, which leads to quenching of fast motions.
source: According to this model, fast motions (e.g., those on a ns timescale) are uncorrelated; an allosteric activator strengths inter-community coupling, which in turn leads to quenching of fast motions.
evidence: This describes a theoretical model from the literature.

claim: The dynamic model of allostery predicts that slower cross-community correlated motions are initiated by an allosteric activator.
source: The model further predicts another dynamic effect, i.e., slower (e.g., μs-ms), cross-community correlated motions are initiated.
evidence: This describes a prediction from a theoretical model.

claim: Chen et al.'s CPMG data for residues around the catalytic center indicated enhanced μs-ms conformational exchange upon trunSUMO1 binding.
source: Indeed, Chen et al.'s CPMG data for residues around the catalytic center indicated enhanced μs-ms conformational exchange upon trunSUMO1 binding (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: The conformational and dynamic effects of β-grasp binding are achieved through increasing the exosite cleft distance and then rigidly holding the two interface regions at the widened separation.
source: The results presented above lead to the hypothesis that the conformational and dynamic effects of β-grasp binding are achieved through increasing the exosite cleft distance and then rigidly holding the two interface regions at the widened separation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the MD simulation results.

claim: The restrained apo simulation reproduces the main conformational and dynamic effects of β-grasp binding.
source: The simulation of this control system reproduces the main conformational and dynamic effects of β-grasp binding.
evidence: This is observed from the restrained MD simulation shown in Figure 6.

claim: The three channel-lining loops in the control system move in essentially the same ways as those in the trunSUMO1-bound form.
source: The three channel-lining loops in the control system move in essentially the same ways as those in the trunSUMO1-bound form (compare Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b with Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is observed from the restrained MD simulation shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The RMSF of the control system shows a similar albeit slightly more pronounced decrease for most of the SENP1 structure.
source: The RMSF of the control system (Figure 6b) also shows a similar albeit slightly more pronounced decrease, indicating quenching of ns dynamics, for most of the SENP1 structure, including all the three channel-lining loops.
evidence: This is observed from the restrained MD simulation shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The calculated backbone amide CSPs of the control system have a similar gradient to that of the trunSUMO1-bound form.
source: Lastly the calculated backbone amide CSPs of the control system have a similar gradient to that of the trunSUMO1-bound form, and the calculated sidechain methyl CSPs again identify two hydrophobic pathways that may propagate allosteric effects from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is observed from CSP calculations on the restrained MD simulation shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The calculated sidechain methyl CSPs of the control system again identify two hydrophobic pathways that may propagate allosteric effects from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center.
source: Lastly the calculated backbone amide CSPs of the control system have a similar gradient to that of the trunSUMO1-bound form, and the calculated sidechain methyl CSPs again identify two hydrophobic pathways that may propagate allosteric effects from the exosite cleft to the catalytic center (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is observed from CSP calculations on the restrained MD simulation shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The wedging into the exosite cleft and the bridging between the two exosite interface regions by the β-grasp domain are the underlying reason for the widened exosite cleft and the quenched fast dynamics.
source: We conclude that the wedging into the exosite cleft and the bridging between the two exosite interface regions by the β-grasp domain are the underlying reason for the widened exosite cleft and the quenched fast dynamics, and may also be the instigator of inter-subdomain slow motions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MD simulation results.

claim: The β-grasp domain may be the instigator of inter-subdomain slow motions.
source: We conclude that the wedging into the exosite cleft and the bridging between the two exosite interface regions by the β-grasp domain are the underlying reason for the widened exosite cleft and the quenched fast dynamics, and may also be the instigator of inter-subdomain slow motions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the MD simulation results and theoretical considerations.

claim: Widening of the exosite cleft may enhance the rate at which the substrate binds to the catalytic center.
source: First, widening of the exosite cleft may enhance the rate at which the substrate binds to the catalytic center, although this effect may not be detectable in an enzymatic assay if the binding does not rate-limit the overall enzymatic reaction.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the observed conformational changes.

claim: Initiation of slow conformational dynamics may facilitate the proper alignment of the substrate around the catalytic residues.
source: Second, initiation of slow conformational dynamics may facilitate the proper alignment of the substrate around the catalytic residues.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the observed dynamic changes.

claim: The putative effects of β-grasp binding can explain the observation that trunSUMO1 enhances the SENP1 catalytic activity on a peptide substrate through increasing kcat.
source: These putative effects can explain the observation of Chen et al. (2014) that trunSUMO1 enhances the SENP1 catalytic activity on a peptide substrate through increasing kcat.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the simulation results to experimental observations.

claim: The binding of a substrate-containing SUMO likely occurs in a sequential manner: the β-grasp domain first wedges into the exosite cleft and the C-terminus then docks into the catalytic channel.
source: The binding of a substrate-containing SUMO (i.e., a precursor or SUMO conjugate) likely occurs in a sequential manner: the β-grasp domain first wedges into the exosite cleft and the C-terminus then docks into the catalytic channel.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on the simulation results.

claim: Tethering can facilitate binding by correctly orienting the C-terminal substrate.
source: Tethering can facilitate this binding by correctly orienting the C-terminal substrate.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about the role of tethering.

claim: Tethering can reinforce the motional coupling between the exosite interface regions and the channel-lining loops.
source: Tethering can also reinforce the motional coupling between the exosite interface regions and the channel-lining loops.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about the role of tethering.

claim: A dock-and-coalesce mechanism describes the binding of intrinsically disordered proteins.
source: In previous studies we have put forward a docking-and-coalesce mechanism to describe the binding of intrinsically disordered proteins, which, similar to the disordered SUMO C-terminus, usually form extended conformations on their targets (Qin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Qin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012.

claim: The wedging of the SUMO β-grasp domain widens the separation between and tightly links the two exosite interface regions.
source: The process starts with the wedging of the SUMO β-grasp domain into the SENP exosite cleft. This wedging widens the separation between and also tightly links the two exosite interface regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation results.

claim: The widening of the exosite cleft enables the docking of the proximal portion of the C-terminus into the catalytic channel.
source: The widening of the exosite cleft enables the docking of the proximal portion of the C-terminus into the catalytic channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation results.

claim: The wedged β-grasp domain strengthens the motional coupling within and between the two subdomains of SENP.
source: Moreover, the wedged β-grasp domain strengthens the motional coupling within and between the two subdomains of SENP, and the newly docked proximal portion of the SUMO C-terminus reinforces this coupling.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation results.

claim: The newly docked proximal portion of the SUMO C-terminus reinforces the motional coupling within and between the two subdomains of SENP.
source: Moreover, the wedged β-grasp domain strengthens the motional coupling within and between the two subdomains of SENP, and the newly docked proximal portion of the SUMO C-terminus reinforces this coupling.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the simulation results.

claim: The strengthened coupling sets up the condition for the emergence of inter-subdomain correlated motions.
source: According to a theoretical model (Guo and Zhou, 2015), the strengthened coupling sets up the condition for the emergence of inter-subdomain correlated motions, which finally allow for the distal portion of the SUMO C-terminus to align properly around the catalytic center for bond cleavage.
evidence: This is based on a theoretical model cited from Guo and Zhou, 2015.

claim: Inter-subdomain correlated motions allow for the distal portion of the SUMO C-terminus to align properly around the catalytic center for bond cleavage.
source: According to a theoretical model (Guo and Zhou, 2015), the strengthened coupling sets up the condition for the emergence of inter-subdomain correlated motions, which finally allow for the distal portion of the SUMO C-terminus to align properly around the catalytic center for bond cleavage.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on a theoretical model.

claim: The catalytic activities of a particular SENP can vary toward different SUMO paralogues.
source: The catalytic activities of a particular SENP can vary toward different SUMO paralogues (Reverter and Lima, 2006; Shen et al., 2006a; Hickey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reverter and Lima, 2006; Shen et al., 2006a; Hickey et al., 2012.

claim: SENP1 processes preSUMO1 and deconjugates SUMO1 and SUMO2 conjugates with similar rates.
source: For example, SENP1 processes preSUMO1 and deconjugates SUMO1 and SUMO2 conjugates with similar rates, but processes the SUMO2 precursor with a 25-fold lower kcat (Shen et al., 2006a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shen et al., 2006a.

claim: SENP1 processes the SUMO2 precursor with a 25-fold lower kcat than preSUMO1.
source: For example, SENP1 processes preSUMO1 and deconjugates SUMO1 and SUMO2 conjugates with similar rates, but processes the SUMO2 precursor with a 25-fold lower kcat (Shen et al., 2006a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shen et al., 2006a.

claim: The decrease in kcat for SENP1 processing of SUMO2 precursor was attributed to a compromised fit between the C-terminal extension and the catalytic channel.
source: The decrease in kcat was attributed to a compromised fit between the C-terminal extension and the catalytic channel.
evidence: This is an interpretation from the literature.

claim: In either processing or deconjugation, SENP2 discriminates between SUMO1 and SUMO2 not by kcat but by KM.
source: On the other hand, in either processing or deconjugation, SENP2 discriminates between SUMO1 and SUMO2 not by kcat but by KM (Reverter and Lima, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reverter and Lima, 2006.

claim: SENP2 has an approximately 10-fold lower KM for SUMO2 than for SUMO1.
source: An approximately 10-fold lower KM for SUMO2 was attributed to an extended exosite interface.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reverter and Lima, 2006.

claim: The lower KM of SENP2 for SUMO2 was attributed to an extended exosite interface.
source: An approximately 10-fold lower KM for SUMO2 was attributed to an extended exosite interface.
evidence: This is an interpretation from the literature.

claim: Stronger electrostatic attraction across the exosite interface quickens the initial wedging of the SUMO2 β-grasp domain into the exosite and slows down the reverse process.
source: First, stronger electrostatic attraction across the exosite interface quickens the initial wedging of the SUMO2 β-grasp domain into the exosite and slows down the reverse process.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: More extensive exosite interactions likely cause stronger allosteric effects of the wedged β-grasp domain, resulting in faster docking of the SUMO2 C-terminus into the catalytic channel.
source: Second, the more extensive exosite interactions likely cause stronger allosteric effects of the wedged β-grasp domain, resulting in faster docking of the SUMO2 C-terminus into the catalytic channel.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The two consequences of more extensive exosite interactions may explain the lower KM for SUMO2 than for SUMO1 in SENP2.
source: These two consequences together may explain the lower KM for SUMO2 than for SUMO1.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: A pre-bound SUMO2, but not SUMO1, β-grasp domain enhanced the SENP2 catalytic activity on a peptide substrate.
source: Here the expectation for stronger allosteric effects is specifically supported by the observation that a pre-bound SUMO2, but not SUMO1, β-grasp domain enhanced the SENP2 catalytic activity on a peptide substrate (Mikolajczyk et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mikolajczyk et al., 2007.

claim: A SENP2 mutant designed by grafting an insertion in the β1-β2 hairpin from SENP6 extended the exosite lower interface and increased the proteolytic activity of SENP2 for some SUMO2 conjugates.
source: A similar causal link between strengthened exosite interactions and strengthened allosteric effects may be at play for a SENP2 mutant that was designed by grafting an insertion in the β1-β2 hairpin from SENP6 (Alegre and Reverter, 2014). The insertion extended the exosite lower interface and increased the proteolytic activity of SENP2 for some SUMO2 conjugates.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alegre and Reverter, 2014.

claim: The exosite may be a potential target site for drug development.
source: The foregoing discussion suggests that the exosite may be another potential target site for drug development.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the study's findings.

claim: Suppression and elevation of SENP activities can be achieved by disrupting and strengthening exosite SENP-SUMO interactions, respectively.
source: Suppression and elevation of SENP activities may both be desired (under different pathological conditions) and can be achieved by disrupting and strengthening exosite SENP-SUMO interactions, respectively.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the study's findings.

claim: Small molecules that bind at sites deeply into the SENP-SUMO interface can have a disruptive effect.
source: Small molecules that bind at sites deeply into the SENP-SUMO interface can have a disruptive effect (Kumar and Zhang, 2013), whereas those bind over both SENP and SUMO can lock and strengthen their interactions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumar and Zhang, 2013.

claim: Small molecules that bind over both SENP and SUMO can lock and strengthen their interactions.
source: Small molecules that bind at sites deeply into the SENP-SUMO interface can have a disruptive effect (Kumar and Zhang, 2013), whereas those bind over both SENP and SUMO can lock and strengthen their interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on structural considerations.
